title: Savoy bell comes down after more than a century
text:
Texoma

Savoy bell comes down after more than a century

BY VICKI GRAVES
HERALD DEMOCRAT

SAVOY — Easing the old church bell with pry bars and pulleys, Savoy ISD maintenance personnel slid it over just enough to make a space for the forklift to go under oak timbers that supported it for 128 years.

One of the school parents, Wendell Moore, operated the sky-cab that lifted it down from the Methodist Church bell tower Wednesday morning. "We chained it like you wouldn't believe because the last thing we wanted was to drop that bronze bell and bust it in a million pieces," said Savoy Superintendent Brian Neal.

COURTESY PHOTO
Wendell Moore carefully removes the bronze bell Wednesday morning from the Savoy Methodist Church bell tower on Fowler Street and takes it to the Savoy ISD maintenance shop for restoration.

The school district will get advice from the manufacturer, which is still in business. Henry McShane Bell Foundry of Baltimore, Md. will give instructions on cleaning the timeworn Savoy keepsake, made in 1876.

Col. William Savoy founded the town and Nancy Savoy, wife of the late John Savoy of Arizona, who was the last remaining grandson, donated $25,000 to Savoy ISD last year. With that money, the school district would restore the bell and establish a $1,000 annual scholarships.

Col. Savoy donated the land for the 1878 Methodist church on Fowler Street. That congregation blended long ago with another church and the school district came into possession of the building, which gradually deteriorated over time. It's the oldest building in Savoy and one of the few that survived the 1878 tornado, Neal said.

Savoy ISD moved the bell from the tower without using any of the $25,000. Nancy Savoy envisioned the 1,000-pound bell would be moved to a place where it could be rung on special occasions, perhaps at one of the schools or at the park. A special committee will decide, Neal said.

The preparation to move it took several hours. "We all held our breaths until it actually came on out of there," he said.

While supervising the operation, Neal talked to one retired gentleman as they watched and mentioned that he wondered how they would get it down. They talked about how church builders probably used mules and pulleys to get it up there because there's just no other way they could have done it. "I guess you're right. If they got it up there in 1878, we should be able to get it down in 2006," Neal said he told the other man.

"We still have all the original money Mrs. Savoy gave us and hope to build the bell a new home and have money left for a scholarship that will last a while."

The school board wanted to move the bell before the building lost its integrity and it fell. "That's a very heavy bell and when you got to ringing it, as I have, you felt the place vibrate. I didn't want to come over after some storm and find it broken and neither did Mrs. Savoy. We wanted to act and get it down," Neal said.

Maintenance people moving it noticed the name "Will[?]" carved into one of oak timbers. Neal also said the rope pull had worn a two-inch-deep rut rubbing on the side of the oak timber, over the years.

A church in Wisconsin offered $3,000 for the church bell, Neal said, "But I'm not going to be the guy who lets that bell get out of Savoy. It's been here 128 years. I guess we're going to leave it here."
